proposedchanges.description_long:
At a White House ceremony on Wednesday, February 11, 2026, Donald Trump received a trophy from the Washington Coal Club, which called him the “undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal.” The Guardian described the club as an advocacy group with financial ties to the coal industry. James Grech, chief executive of Peabody Energy, presented the award and thanked Trump for actions supporting the industry. More than a dozen coal executives and miners attended.

The ceremony coincided with Trump signing an executive order directing the Defense Department to secure long-term power purchase agreements with coal plants for military installations and other “mission-critical facilities.” Trump also announced that the Energy Department would allocate $175 million to six projects to modernize, retrofit, and extend coal plants serving rural and remote communities. The ceremony placed the award alongside the administration’s coal policy announcements. The report did not identify executed Pentagon contracts or project outcomes.

proposedchanges.description_medium: On February 12, 2026, the Trump administration announced that the EPA would rescind the 2009 endangerment finding, which says greenhouse gases threaten public health and welfare. The finding underpinned federal climate rules, including vehicle standards. Health and environmental groups sued, arguing the repeal discarded evidence about those risks. The litigation left the action’s legal status contested.
proposedchanges.description_long:
The EPA’s 2009 endangerment finding concluded that greenhouse gases threaten public health and welfare, giving the agency a basis to regulate emissions under the Clean Air Act. On February 12, 2026, the Trump administration announced that the EPA would rescind the finding and withdraw federal greenhouse-gas standards for motor vehicles. The finding had supported a broad set of federal climate rules, so its removal put the legal basis for those rules at issue.

More than a dozen health and environmental groups sued the EPA, arguing that the repeal discarded the agency’s earlier assessment of greenhouse-gas risks. Harvard’s Salata Institute described the action as part of the administration’s wider effort to reduce federal climate regulation. The lawsuit contested the repeal, but the supplied reporting does not establish how courts will rule or quantify future emissions. The announcement and legal challenge document the immediate policy change and response, while the longer-term regulatory effect remains unresolved.

evidencebasis: The assigned packet identifies the proposed rescission, withdrawn vehicle standards, the finding’s role in climate rules, and litigation by health and environmental groups. Both supplied source URLs remain unchanged.

proposedchanges.description_long:
Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s border czar, said in a June 2025 NBC interview that immigration enforcement should prioritize people with criminal records. He argued that keeping to that priority would preserve public support and added that enforcement should be humane. The Guardian highlighted those remarks after Homan was sent to Minnesota in January 2026, following federal agents’ fatal shootings of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

The article contrasted Homan’s earlier call for targeted enforcement with the administration’s wider operations. It reported that federal agents had arrested hundreds of thousands of people, including U.S. citizens, and cited figures showing fewer than 14% of almost 400,000 immigrants arrested by ICE in the first year of Trump’s second presidency had charges or convictions for violent offenses. That figure challenged the administration’s repeated claim that it focused on “the worst of the worst.” Homan’s interview documents his stated approach; it does not establish that ICE consistently followed it.

proposedchanges.title: Gil Dezer’s Jet Used in ICE Deportations of Palestinian Men to the West Bank
proposedchanges.description_short: Gil Dezer’s Jet Used in ICE Deportations of Palestinian Men to the West Bank
proposedchanges.description_medium: A Guardian investigation linked two ICE deportation flights to a private jet owned by Florida developer Gil Dezer. The first flight carried eight Palestinian men from Arizona to Tel Aviv on January 21, 2026; Israeli authorities later left them at a West Bank checkpoint. ICE chartered the aircraft through Journey Aviation. Dezer said he did not know the passengers or purpose of privately chartered trips.
proposedchanges.description_long:
On January 21, 2026, a private Gulfstream jet owned by Florida developer Gil Dezer flew eight Palestinian men from Arizona to Tel Aviv as part of an ICE deportation operation, The Guardian reported. Israeli authorities later left the men at a West Bank checkpoint. Local residents helped them contact relatives and arrange transportation. One of the deported men, Maher Awad, told the newspaper that he had lived in the United States for nearly a decade.

The same aircraft carried another group of Palestinian deportees on a second flight later that month. ICE chartered the jet through Journey Aviation, a company that also charters aircraft to U.S. agencies. The Guardian identified Dezer as a longtime Trump business partner and donor and as a friend of Donald Trump Jr. Dezer said he was not told the names of passengers or the purpose of privately chartered trips. The article reports that U.S. officials did not answer questions about the flights’ cost. It documents the aircraft’s use and Dezer’s business ties, but does not show that Dezer, Trump, or Trump Jr. arranged the deportations.

evidencebasis: The linked Guardian investigation identifies Gil Dezer, the aircraft, Journey Aviation, the January flight, the deported men’s arrival, and Dezer’s stated lack of passenger and trip-purpose information. The source URL remains unchanged.
